patient.name: Bernadette O'Sullivan
patient.complaint: Right knee pain for 18 months, worse on walking
background: Retired school dinner lady from Croydon

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an older, overweight patient with activity-related joint pain, short morning stiffness, crepitus and normal inflammatory markers, or hand OA with Heberden's nodes versus rheumatoid.

points: Bernadette, 67: right knee **aches after walking** to the shops.
Eases with rest; worse by evening.
Stiff for about **10 minutes** on getting up.
No fever, no weight loss, no hot red joint.

steps.lead: Bernadette's knee is wearing out: **cartilage degeneration** with osteophytes and a low-grade effusion, not an inflammatory arthritis.
Her **BMI of 34** is her biggest modifiable risk factor; age over 50 and both knees aching fit primary OA.

visual.title: Morning stiffness
visual.label: Bernadette 10 min
visual.caption: Short stiffness after rest points to OA; long morning stiffness points to an inflammatory arthritis.

points: Right knee: **crepitus**, small cool effusion.
Slightly reduced flexion; mild **varus** deformity.
**Antalgic gait**: short stance on the right.
No warmth or redness.

steps.lead: Activity pain, stiffness under 30 minutes, crepitus and **no fever or erythema**: Bernadette's knee is classic OA.

steps.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis for Bernadette's knee?
steps.r: Chronic activity-related pain, short stiffness and crepitus in an older obese woman is **osteoarthritis**. Gout and sepsis are acute and hot.

points: Hands: hard bony swellings at the **DIP** joints.
Similar smaller swellings at the **PIP** joints.
Base of both thumbs looks **squared**.
MCP joints and wrists spared.

steps.lead: Bernadette's DIP lumps are **Heberden's nodes** and her PIP lumps are **Bouchard's nodes**. DIP involvement argues against rheumatoid.

steps.title: Osteoarthritis vs rheumatoid arthritis
head: Feature
Osteoarthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis
rows: Worse after rest, improves with use

steps.lead: A year later Bernadette develops sudden pain behind the knee and a bruised, swollen calf: a **ruptured Baker's cyst**.

steps.text: A ruptured Baker's cyst looks like a **DVT**: swollen, tender calf. Look for **bruising around the ankle**, and still exclude DVT with a Doppler ultrasound.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate investigation?' where the answer is often none: OA is a clinical diagnosis over 45. Or 'Which is the most likely X-ray finding?' (loss of joint space, osteophytes, subchondral cysts, sclerosis).

steps.q: Bernadette asks for a scan to confirm it. Which is most appropriate?
steps.r: Over 45, activity-related pain and stiffness under 30 minutes: **clinical diagnosis**. Imaging is not needed to diagnose typical OA.

steps.lead: Bernadette meets all three NICE criteria: **over 45**, activity-related pain, stiffness **under 30 minutes**. No test is needed.

visual.title: Age criterion for clinical diagnosis
visual.label: Bernadette 67
visual.caption: A younger patient with unilateral OA needs a reason, such as a previous injury.

steps.title: Bloods taken for her hands
steps.text: All normal, as expected in OA.
**Normal inflammatory markers** are part of the OA picture. A raised CRP should make you think of an inflammatory, crystal or septic arthritis.

points: Two years on, pain is severe despite treatment.
Knee X-ray before orthopaedic referral.

steps.lead: Bernadette's X-ray shows the four classic signs: **loss of joint space**, **osteophytes**, **subchondral cysts** and **subarticular sclerosis**.

steps.title: OA X-ray signs: LOSS
steps.caption: Compare: punched-out erosions in gout, chondrocalcinosis in pseudogout, osteopenia in rheumatoid.

steps.text: X-ray severity matches symptoms poorly. Do not X-ray to **diagnose** typical OA; use it when the picture is atypical or before surgery.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' for knee OA: topical NSAID plus exercise first, oral NSAID with a PPI next, steroid injection for flares, and arthroplasty for severe disease.

steps.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment for Bernadette's knee?
steps.r: First-line knee OA is a **topical NSAID** plus **exercise/physiotherapy** and weight loss. Routine paracetamol is no longer offered.

steps.lead: Bernadette starts **topical diclofenac** gel and a physio-led exercise programme. Her eGFR of 78 and few vascular risks mean NSAIDs are allowed.

points: Three months later: still painful walking to the shops.
GP adds **oral naproxen**.
She has no ulcer history.

steps.lead: Every OA patient on an oral NSAID gets a **PPI**, so Bernadette has omeprazole with her naproxen. With CKD she would get lifestyle advice instead.

visual.title: Bernadette's knee pain score
visual.caption: The steroid injection works well but wears off; arthroplasty gives lasting relief.

steps.lead: In a bad flare Bernadette has an **intra-articular methylprednisolone** injection: effective but **temporary**, as the trend shows.

points: Two years on: night pain, walking under 100 metres.
Function poor despite full conservative treatment.
Referred for **total knee replacement**.

steps.lead: Bernadette's severe, refractory disease needs **arthroplasty**. After a knee replacement the **common peroneal nerve** is most at risk (foot drop).

steps.title: Shortened, rotated leg: which is it?
head: Posterior hip prosthesis dislocation
Fractured neck of femur

steps.text: The most common reason for hip replacement **revision** is **aseptic loosening**.

steps.lead: Bernadette's clinical diagnosis and stepwise plan follow the **NICE osteoarthritis guideline**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions on why cartilage is lost (MMP breakdown exceeding repair), why osteophytes form, or why a ruptured Baker's cyst mimics a DVT.

steps.lead: In Bernadette's knee, **matrix metalloproteinase** breakdown of cartilage outpaces repair, so the cartilage thins year by year.

steps.title: From load to an osteoarthritic knee
nodes: Articular cartilage thins: joint space narrows
Subchondral bone remodels: sclerosis and cysts

steps.lead: Bernadette's osteophytes and sclerosis are her bone's **attempted repair** as the cartilage cushion is lost.

steps.q: Why is Bernadette's CRP normal despite a knee effusion?
o: The effusion is blood, not fluid
steps.r: Cartilage debris causes **low-grade local synovitis** without the systemic response of inflammatory arthritis, so CRP stays normal.

steps.lead: Bernadette's small effusion is **low-grade synovitis** from cartilage debris, so she has swelling without fever or a raised CRP.

visual.title: Bernadette's BMI
visual.label: Bernadette 34
visual.caption: Every extra kilogram adds several kilograms of load across the knee with each step.

steps.lead: Bernadette's weight increases **mechanical loading** of her knees; in a younger patient an old meniscal or ligament injury does the same.
Bernadette's Baker's cyst was synovial fluid herniating into the **popliteal fossa**; rupture spilled it into her calf, mimicking a DVT.

steps.text: OA is a **non-inflammatory** arthritis: the damage is mechanical and degenerative, so treatment targets load, pain and function, not the immune system.

mcq.q: Which is one of the strongest risk factors for osteoarthritis?
mcq.r: **Obesity** increases mechanical loading of weight-bearing joints.

mcq.q: Which hand joints are typically affected by osteoarthritis?
mcq.r: OA affects **DIP and PIP** joints and the thumb base; rheumatoid spares the DIPs.

mcq.q: Which complication of knee OA can mimic a DVT?
mcq.r: A ruptured **Baker's cyst** gives posterior knee pain and calf swelling with bruising.

mcq.q: How long is morning stiffness in osteoarthritis?
mcq.r: OA stiffness is **under 30 minutes**; over an hour suggests inflammatory arthritis.

mcq.q: Which is NOT a classic X-ray feature of osteoarthritis?
mcq.r: Periarticular osteopenia is **rheumatoid**. OA shows LOSS: joint space loss, osteophytes, subchondral cysts, sclerosis.

mcq.q: What is first-line drug treatment for knee osteoarthritis?
mcq.r: **Topical NSAID** plus exercise. Routine paracetamol should not be offered.

mcq.q: What must be co-prescribed with an oral NSAID in OA?
mcq.r: NICE: co-prescribe a **PPI** with oral NSAIDs in all OA patients.

mcq.q: Which nerve is most at risk in knee arthroplasty?
mcq.r: The **common peroneal nerve**, causing foot drop.

mcq.q: Which enzymes drive cartilage breakdown in OA?
mcq.r: **Matrix metalloproteinases** break down cartilage faster than it is repaired.

glossary.Osteoarthritis: Degenerative joint disease with cartilage loss, bony overgrowth and low-grade inflammation.
glossary.Articular cartilage: Smooth tissue covering bone ends inside a joint, allowing frictionless movement.
glossary.Osteophytes: Bony spurs at the edges of a joint, formed as the bone tries to repair itself.
glossary.Synovitis: Inflammation of the synovial lining of a joint.
glossary.Effusion: Excess fluid inside a joint, causing swelling.
glossary.Stenosing tenosynovitis: Narrowing and inflammation of a tendon sheath, as in trigger finger.
glossary.Crepitus: A grating or crackling sensation felt or heard when a rough joint moves.
glossary.Antalgic gait: A limp in which the patient spends less time on the painful leg.
glossary.Varus: Deformity with the knee pointing outwards, giving a bow-legged look.
glossary.Valgus: Deformity with the knee pointing inwards, giving a knock-kneed look.
glossary.DIP: Distal interphalangeal joint, the finger joint nearest the fingertip.
glossary.PIP: Proximal interphalangeal joint, the middle finger joint.
glossary.MCP: Metacarpophalangeal joint, the knuckle joint; typical in rheumatoid arthritis.
glossary.Carpometacarpal joint: Joint between wrist bones and hand bones; the first one is at the base of the thumb.
glossary.Heberden's nodes: Hard bony swellings of the DIP joints in osteoarthritis.
glossary.Bouchard's nodes: Hard bony swellings of the PIP joints in osteoarthritis.
glossary.Squaring of the thumb: Square-looking thumb base caused by osteoarthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint.
glossary.Baker's cyst: A fluid-filled swelling behind the knee from synovial fluid herniating into the popliteal fossa.
glossary.Popliteal fossa: The diamond-shaped hollow at the back of the knee.
glossary.DVT: Deep vein thrombosis, a blood clot in a deep leg vein.
glossary.Subchondral cysts: Fluid-filled holes in the bone just beneath damaged cartilage, seen on X-ray.
glossary.Subarticular sclerosis: Increased bone density beneath the joint surface, seen as a whiter band on X-ray.
glossary.Topical NSAID: An anti-inflammatory gel or cream, such as diclofenac, applied over the joint.
glossary.PPI: Proton pump inhibitor, such as omeprazole, which protects the stomach from NSAIDs.
glossary.Celecoxib: A COX-2 selective NSAID with less stomach irritation.
glossary.Intra-articular: Injected directly into the joint space.
glossary.Methylprednisolone: A corticosteroid used for joint injections.
glossary.Common peroneal nerve: Nerve winding round the fibular neck; injury causes foot drop.
glossary.Aseptic loosening: Loosening of a joint replacement without infection; the commonest reason for hip revision.
glossary.Matrix metalloproteinases: Enzymes that break down cartilage matrix; overactive in osteoarthritis.
glossary.Meniscus: C-shaped cartilage cushion in the knee; tears predispose to later OA.
glossary.CKD: Chronic kidney disease, in which NSAIDs are best avoided.
glossary.Revision: A repeat operation to replace or fix a failed joint replacement.
glossary.De Quervain's tenosynovitis: Inflammation of thumb tendons at the wrist, causing radial wrist pain; a differential for thumb base OA.

technique.stem: A 69 year old woman has an 18 month history of pain in both knees, worse after walking and relieved by rest. Her knees are stiff for 15 minutes in the morning. Her BMI is 33. Both knees have crepitus and small cool effusions. She has bony swellings of the distal interphalangeal joints of both hands.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about chronic joint pain: mechanical or inflammatory?

clues: worse after walking and relieved by rest
steps.x: Chronic, activity-related, short stiffness, obese, crepitus and DIP nodes (Heberden's).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Mechanical pain plus Heberden's nodes: **osteoarthritis**.

elim: Bursitis is a localised soft tissue swelling, not bilateral joint disease with nodes.
Gout is acute and hot, classically the big toe.
A meniscal tear follows twisting injury, with locking, usually one knee.
Rheumatoid has long morning stiffness and spares the DIP joints.

steps.x: **D. Osteoarthritis.** Rule: activity pain + stiffness under 30 min + DIP nodes = OA.

technique.stem: A 63 year old man has a 1 year history of right knee pain that comes on with walking. He has 10 minutes of stiffness on waking. There is crepitus on movement and no warmth. He is otherwise well and asks what test is needed to confirm the diagnosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No test is needed: **clinical diagnosis**.

elim: Inflammatory markers are not needed when the picture is typical.
MRI is not used to diagnose OA.
Rheumatoid factor tests for rheumatoid arthritis, which this is not.
X-ray is not needed for typical OA and correlates poorly with symptoms.

steps.x: **A. Clinical diagnosis.** Rule: over 45 + activity pain + stiffness under 30 min = OA, no imaging.

technique.stem: A 66 year old woman has knee osteoarthritis. She has used topical diclofenac and done physiotherapy for 3 months but still has pain on walking. She has no history of peptic ulcer disease or kidney disease. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.

steps.x: Next step after first-line has failed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Oral NSAID **with a PPI**.

elim: Opioids are not the next step in OA.
NICE requires a PPI with every oral NSAID in OA.
Routine paracetamol is not offered.
Arthroplasty is for severe, refractory disease, not after 3 months.

steps.x: **B. Oral naproxen with omeprazole.** Rule: oral NSAID always with a PPI.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man has a knee X-ray for long-standing osteoarthritis. It shows narrowing of the joint space with bony spurs at the joint margins and dense white bone beneath the articular surface.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the bony spurs?
o: Attempted repair by remodelling subchondral bone

steps.x: A mechanism question: why do osteophytes form in OA?

clues: bony spurs at the joint margins
steps.x: Joint space loss, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis: classic OA.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Bone remodels as **attempted repair** after cartilage loss.

elim: CPP deposition gives chondrocalcinosis in pseudogout.
Osteoclast activation causes bone loss, not new bone.
Pannus causes erosions in rheumatoid arthritis.
Urate deposition gives punched-out erosions in gout.

steps.x: **A. Attempted repair by remodelling.** Rule: osteophytes and sclerosis = bone's repair response to cartilage loss.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman has a 2 year history of left knee pain that is worse at the end of the day and after walking. Morning stiffness lasts 15 minutes. Her BMI is 35. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 136/84 mmHg. The knee has crepitus and a small cool effusion.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Chronic activity-related knee pain with short stiffness, crepitus, obesity and normal inflammatory markers is osteoarthritis. Crystal and septic arthritis present acutely with a hot joint.

clues: worse at the end of the day and after walking
steps.x: Chronic, mechanical, short stiffness, obese, normal CRP.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Osteoarthritis**.

Pseudogout is an acute hot knee.
Rheumatoid has long stiffness and raised markers.

steps.x: **B. Osteoarthritis.** Rule: chronic + mechanical + normal CRP = OA.

practice.stem: A 64 year old woman has aching fingers for 5 years, worse after gardening. Stiffness lasts 10 minutes in the morning. Her temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. The GP suspects osteoarthritis of the hands.

Bony swellings of the distal interphalangeal joints

Chronic, activity-related, short stiffness.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman has a 6 month history of pain at the base of her right thumb when opening jars and turning keys. The base of the thumb looks square. Pain is reproduced by grinding the thumb metacarpal against the trapezium. Finkelstein's test is negative and sensation in the hand is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Thumb base pain with gripping, squaring and a positive grind test is first CMC joint OA. De Quervain's gives a positive Finkelstein's test.

steps.x: Diagnosis of thumb base pain.

clues: grinding the thumb metacarpal against the trapezium
steps.x: Pain gripping and turning, squaring, positive grind, negative Finkelstein's.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **First CMC joint OA**.

elim: Carpal tunnel causes numbness in the median nerve distribution; sensation is normal.
De Quervain's has a positive Finkelstein's test.
Rheumatoid is a symmetrical MCP/PIP polyarthritis.
No trauma; scaphoid fracture follows a fall on an outstretched hand.

steps.x: **C. First CMC joint OA.** Rule: squared thumb + grip pain = CMC OA.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man with long-standing knee osteoarthritis has sudden pain behind his right knee followed by a swollen, tender right calf. There is bruising around the right ankle. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 140/82 mmHg.
labs: No deep vein thrombus; fluid tracking into the calf
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Sudden posterior knee pain then calf swelling and ankle bruising in knee OA, with no thrombus on Doppler, is a ruptured Baker's cyst.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a swollen calf in a patient with knee OA.

clues: sudden pain behind his right knee
steps.x: OA effusion, posterior knee pain, calf bruising, and Doppler shows no clot.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ruptured Baker's cyst**.

elim: Cellulitis gives fever and spreading erythema.
Doppler shows no thrombus.
Aneurysm is a pulsatile popliteal mass, not sudden calf fluid.
Thrombophlebitis is a tender red superficial vein.

steps.x: **D. Ruptured Baker's cyst.** Rule: OA knee + calf swelling + bruising + no DVT = Baker's.

practice.stem: A 36 year old man has a 2 year history of right knee pain on running and squatting, with slight swelling. His left knee is normal. practice.stem: A 74 year old woman had a total hip replacement for osteoarthritis 2 weeks ago. While bending to put on her shoes she felt a 'clunk' and severe hip pain. She cannot weight-bear. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 148/86 mmHg. The right leg is shortened and internally rotated.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: A clunk on hip flexion soon after hip replacement with a shortened, internally rotated leg is posterior dislocation. Aseptic loosening is a late, gradual cause of revision.

steps.x: Diagnosis of an acute complication after hip arthroplasty for OA.

clues: bending to put on her shoes
steps.x: Early, flexion movement, clunk, short internally rotated leg.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Posterior dislocation**.

elim: Aseptic loosening is late and gradual, years later.
Fracture usually follows a fall; no clunk on bending.

Nerve injury gives foot drop or numbness, not a rotated short leg.

steps.x: **C. Posterior dislocation.** Rule: clunk + short + internally rotated = dislocated hip prosthesis.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man has severe right knee pain despite topical and oral NSAIDs and a steroid injection. He is being referred to orthopaedics. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg. A knee X-ray is requested.

practice.stem: A 65 year old woman has knee osteoarthritis. A biopsy of the articular cartilage taken during her knee replacement shows thinning, fissuring and loss of matrix. There is no pannus or crystal deposition. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her cartilage loss?
practice.e: OA cartilage loss is an imbalance between breakdown by matrix metalloproteinases and repair. Pannus is rheumatoid; urate crystals are gout.

steps.x: Mechanism of cartilage loss in OA.

clues: thinning, fissuring and loss of matrix
steps.x: Degenerative matrix loss without inflammation or crystals, and CRP is normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **MMP breakdown outpacing repair**.

elim: Autoantibodies are not the mechanism in OA.
Immune complexes cause SLE-type disease.
There is no pannus; that is rheumatoid.
There are no crystals; that is gout.

steps.x: **C. MMP breakdown exceeding repair.** Rule: OA = enzyme breakdown beats repair.
